articles.title: What Happens to a Person's Property After Death in Sri Lanka?
articles.seo: Succession Law in Sri Lanka: Property After Death
articles.description: Understand what happens to property after death in Sri Lanka, including inheritance rights, last wills and estate administration.
articles.dek: A clear introduction to inheritance, last wills and the legal steps families may need to take.
sections: What Is Succession?

Succession is the process through which a deceased person's property passes to those legally entitled to receive it. The property and relevant financial obligations left behind are generally called the deceased's estate.

An estate may include houses, land, vehicles, bank accounts, investments, company shares and valuable belongings. However, a person can generally pass on only property or legal interests that actually belonged to them. If they owned half a house, the other half does not become part of their estate simply because they died.

Some assets may need separate examination because of nominations, insurance arrangements or other legally recognised interests. The first step is to find out exactly what property the deceased owned.
What Happens If There Is No Last Will?

When someone dies without a legally effective will covering their property, the applicable law decides who inherits. This is called intestate succession.

Suppose a father dies leaving a wife, two children and a house, but no will. The family cannot simply assume the house belongs entirely to the mother or eldest child. Under Sri Lanka's general law, the surviving spouse ordinarily receives one-half of the deceased's intestate property, and the remainder passes to the other entitled heirs. Special inheritance laws may lead to a different result.
What Happens If There Is a Last Will?

A person may make a last will identifying who should receive property after death. This is known as testate succession. A mother, for example, might leave her house to one child and another property to someone else.

Sri Lankan law recognises broad freedom to decide how property should be distributed by a valid will. But the will must meet legal requirements, and the estate must be administered through the applicable process.
Does Everyone Follow the Same Inheritance Law?

No. Sri Lanka has a general inheritance law and special systems including Kandyan law, Thesawalamai and Muslim law. Which applies depends on legally relevant circumstances. The same inheritance formula cannot safely be used for every family.
What Happens to the Deceased's Debts?

Loans, mortgages and other legally enforceable liabilities must be considered before distribution. A house worth Rs. 20 million may still be subject to a mortgage. Relatives do not ordinarily become personally responsible for every debt merely by inheriting, although separate liability may arise for a co-borrower or guarantor.
Does the Family Have to Go to Court?

Depending on the estate, probate, letters of administration or certificates of heirship may be necessary. These documents address authority to administer the estate or recognition of the heirs. A legal right to inherit does not automatically mean a person can immediately sell the inherited land.

The Civil Procedure Code regulates important testamentary proceedings. Court documentation and the right to inherit are related, but they are not the same question.
What Should the Family Do First?

1. Locate any last will.
  2. Identify the deceased's property and debts.
  3. Gather deeds, financial records, birth, marriage and death certificates.
  4. Identify possible heirs and the law that applies.
  5. Check whether court proceedings are needed before transferring property.
Conclusion

Inheritance is not always a simple division among surviving relatives. Whether a will exists, which law applies, who survives the deceased and what property they owned can all change the outcome. Understanding these matters early helps families protect their rights and avoid unnecessary disputes.
legal: Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance, Part III
articles.intro: When someone dies, what happens to the house they lived in, the land they owned, and the money in their bank accounts? Does everything belong to the surviving husband or wife? Are the children entitled to equal shares? What happens if the person never made a last will? These are questions many Sri Lankan families face, often during an already difficult time. The answers depend on succession law.

articles.title: Who Inherits Property When Someone Dies Without a Will in Sri Lanka?
articles.seo: Who Inherits Without a Will in Sri Lanka?
articles.description: Learn who inherits property when someone dies without a will in Sri Lanka, including the rights of spouses, children and other relatives.
articles.dek: Understand the shares of a surviving spouse, children and other family members under the general law.
sections: What Is Intestate Succession?

If a person dies without a legally effective will disposing of property, the applicable law determines who inherits it. This is called intestate succession. In Sri Lanka, the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance governs general-law intestacy, but different rules may apply under Kandyan law, Thesawalamai or Muslim law.
How Much Does the Surviving Husband or Wife Inherit?

Under section 22 of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance, a surviving spouse ordinarily inherits one-half of the deceased spouse's intestate property. The other half passes to the remaining legal heirs under the statutory rules.

Example: A father dies leaving a wife, two children and a net distributable estate worth Rs. 12 million. Assuming general law applies:

Family memberShareValue
Wife1/2Rs. 6 million
First child1/4Rs. 3 million
Second child1/4Rs. 3 million

The same general principle applies to a husband surviving his wife. The calculation concerns the deceased person's property, not the surviving spouse's separately owned property.
Do Sons and Daughters Inherit Equally?

Under general law, children ordinarily inherit equally. The eldest son does not automatically receive more, and a married daughter does not lose her general-law inheritance rights because of marriage. If a mother dies leaving three children and no spouse, the children ordinarily receive one-third each. Adoption, parentage and special-law questions can require separate examination.

A daughter does not lose these rights simply because she married. The legal position may need separate examination where adoption, legal parentage or a special succession law is involved.
What If One Child Died Before the Parent?

Grandchildren may inherit the share that their deceased parent would have received. Suppose a grandmother had two children, one alive and the other deceased leaving two children. If the grandmother leaves no surviving spouse, the living child ordinarily receives half, and the two grandchildren share the other half. This is called inheritance by representation.
What If the Deceased Had No Children?

Parents may inherit where there are no descendants; siblings may also inherit in certain circumstances. If a person leaves a spouse, no descendants and two surviving parents, the spouse ordinarily receives one-half, with the parents sharing the remainder. The rules are more detailed if only one parent survives or there are full and half-siblings.

Where only one parent survives, the relevant parent may share with certain brothers or sisters under section 25 of the Ordinance. Full and half-siblings can be treated differently. The whole family relationship should therefore be established before distributing property.
What If Only a Husband or Wife Survives?

Having no children does not automatically mean the surviving spouse receives everything. Parents, siblings or other qualifying relatives may have rights. If the relevant classes of other heirs fail, the surviving spouse may become entitled to the entire estate under the general law.
Can an Heir Sell the Inherited House?

Not necessarily. Several heirs may own undivided shares in one house or plot of land. This does not automatically divide the property into physical portions. One heir cannot ordinarily sell the entire property simply because they inherited a share; title and testamentary requirements must be checked.
What Should the Family Do?

Identify all potential heirs, inspect deeds and family records, establish the applicable law and consider whether a court grant or certificate is necessary. Where there are debts or disagreements about shares, obtain advice before distributing or transferring property.

A birth certificate, marriage certificate, death certificate and any adoption order may be relevant. Disagreements should be addressed before an heir attempts to sell more than the share legally belonging to them.
Conclusion

Under Sri Lanka's general law, a surviving spouse ordinarily receives one-half of the intestate estate. Children and other relatives inherit according to the statutory order. The precise result depends on the family relationships, property and law applicable to the deceased.
legal: Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance, sections 21–36
articles.intro: Imagine that a father dies leaving a wife, two children and a house. He never made a last will. Who owns the house now? Does the wife receive everything? Do the children have equal rights? Can the eldest son claim a larger share? Under Sri Lanka's general inheritance law, the answers may be different from what family members expect.

articles.title: What Happens When Someone Dies Leaving a Last Will in Sri Lanka?
articles.seo: Last Will and Inheritance in Sri Lanka
articles.description: Find out what happens when someone dies leaving a last will in Sri Lanka, including beneficiaries, executors and probate.
articles.dek: Learn what a will does, who can benefit, and why an executor may need probate.
sections: What Is a Last Will?

A last will is a legal document stating how a person's property should pass after death. The person making it is the testator; those receiving benefits are beneficiaries; and the person appointed to administer the estate is an executor.

For example, a father may leave a house to his wife, land to a child and money to another beneficiary.

A will may give specified assets to particular beneficiaries, name percentages of the estate, or include other lawful directions. Unlike a lifetime transfer of property, its testamentary directions generally take effect when the testator dies.
Can a Parent Leave Everything to One Child?

Under the Wills Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 29 of 2022, a person has broad freedom to choose beneficiaries. The law expressly recognises exclusion of particular relatives, including children, without giving reasons. A will is not automatically invalid because one child receives more than another. But the document must be valid, and the testator cannot ordinarily dispose of property that belongs to someone else.

That freedom does not remove the need to show the will was genuine or that the testator had the necessary understanding and acted freely when making it.
How Is a Valid Will Made?

Under the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, as amended in 2022, an ordinary will is executed with prescribed signature and impression requirements before a notary public and two witnesses present at the same time. Relevant notarial requirements must also be met. Simply signing a handwritten or typed paper at home is not a reliable substitute.
What Does the Executor Do?

The executor administers the estate in accordance with the will and the law: locating property, addressing enforceable debts, applying for probate when required and distributing the remaining property. Appointment as executor does not mean the person personally inherits the whole estate.
Does the Will Have to Go Before a Court?

A will generally has to be proved through the testamentary procedure commonly called probate. A beneficiary should not assume inherited land can be sold or transferred immediately merely because their name appears in the will.
Can Someone Challenge the Will?

Yes, on recognised legal grounds such as forgery, unlawful pressure, lack of testamentary capacity or improper execution. Disappointment with the inheritance alone is not enough to establish invalidity.
What If the Will Does Not Mention Everything?

Property not effectively disposed of by a will may pass under the applicable intestacy rules. This is called partial intestacy. A carefully drafted provision dealing with the remaining estate can help avoid uncertainty.

A residuary clause is often used to cover assets not specifically mentioned, including property acquired after the will was made.
Conclusion
A last will lets someone decide how legally disposable property should pass after death. Its execution, validity and proper administration remain essential.
legal: Wills Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 29 of 2022
Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 30 of 2022
articles.intro: A mother owns a house and several plots of land. Before her death, she makes a last will leaving the house to one daughter and the land to her other children. After her death, someone in the family argues that all the children must receive equal shares. Is that correct? Not necessarily. Sri Lankan law allows a person to decide how their property should be distributed after death through a legally valid last will.

articles.title: Probate, Letters of Administration and Certificates of Heirship in Sri Lanka: What Is the Difference?
articles.seo: Probate and Estate Administration in Sri Lanka
articles.description: Understand the differences between probate, letters of administration and certificates of heirship under Sri Lankan law.
articles.dek: Three important legal documents explained in everyday language.
sections: What Is Probate?

Probate is a court grant associated with a deceased person's valid last will. Where the will appoints an executor, the executor may apply to the appropriate District Court to have it proved and receive authority to administer the estate.

For example, if a mother leaves a house to her daughter, the executor may need probate before the property can be dealt with through the required legal process.
What Are Letters of Administration?

Letters of administration authorise a person, called the administrator, to deal with a deceased person's estate. They are commonly obtained where no will exists. Letters may also be granted with the will annexed if a will exists but a suitable person other than an executor obtaining probate must act.

The administrator identifies assets, deals with valid debts and distributes property according to law. The grant does not make the administrator the sole beneficial owner.
What Is a Certificate of Heirship?

A certificate of heirship is a court-issued document identifying heirs. In appropriate intestate cases, certificates may identify heirs and their agreed shares. They are not a substitute for active estate administration in every case; the court may decide letters of administration are necessary.
Which Court Should the Family Approach?

These applications generally come before the appropriate District Court. Jurisdiction depends on statutory connections such as the deceased's residence, the applicant's residence or the location of estate land.

Applying in the wrong court or without necessary information can delay dealing with property. Court jurisdiction should be checked before filing.
Does the Value of the Estate Matter?

Yes. The Civil Procedure Code contains requirements for certain intestate estates valued at Rs. 4 million or more. Section 525 imposes a reporting duty on the surviving spouse or next of kin where a person dies in Sri Lanka without a will and leaves property in Sri Lanka meeting the statutory threshold.

But the threshold does not mean every smaller estate is free from court procedure or transfer documentation.
What If Someone Objects?

Interested persons may object to an application through the prescribed process, for example disputing a will or the applicant's entitlement to administer the estate. The court may need to resolve disputed facts before issuing the grant.

A person may dispute the identity of an heir, the validity of a will, or who should act as administrator. An objection may require an inquiry and does not automatically establish that the objector is correct.
Can Inherited Property Be Sold Immediately?

Not always. Section 545 of the Civil Procedure Code restricts certain transfers. The relevant period, value, existence of a will and available court documents can affect whether a transfer is permitted. Obtain title and succession advice before selling inherited land.

Even when the family agrees on a sale, the purchaser may need reliable documents proving both the seller's title and any required authority to deal with the deceased's estate.
Conclusion
Probate, administration and certificates of heirship have different purposes. Establish whether a will exists, identify the estate and heirs, and then determine the correct procedure.
articles.intro: A father dies leaving a house and money in a bank account. His wife and children know that they may be entitled to inherit. However, when they try to deal with the property, they are told that legal documents are required. They hear three expressions: probate, letters of administration and certificates of heirship. What do they mean, and which one might the family need?

articles.title: What Property Forms Part of a Deceased Person's Estate in Sri Lanka?
articles.seo: What Property Forms Part of an Estate?
articles.description: Learn which assets form part of a deceased person's estate, including jointly owned property, bank deposits, gifts and debts.
articles.dek: Before calculating inheritance shares, find out which assets the deceased actually owned.
sections: What Is Included in an Estate?

When someone dies, relatives often ask who should inherit the house or savings. But the first question is what property actually belonged to the deceased?

An estate may include land, houses, vehicles, bank balances, investments, company shares, valuables and business rights. Ownership, mortgages, trusts and nominations may change the position.

It may also include money owed to the deceased and certain rights connected with a business. Not every asset associated with the deceased forms part of the estate that can be divided immediately. Establish the legal basis of ownership.
What If the House Belonged to Both Husband and Wife?

Suppose a husband and wife own a house worth Rs. 20 million in equal shares. The husband dies without a will, leaving his wife and two children. The wife's existing half-share does not become part of the husband's estate. Only the husband's half-share is inherited.

Assuming the general law applies and there are no complicating circumstances:

PersonFinal share of house
Wife3/4
First child1/8
Second child1/8

The wife keeps her own half and inherits half of her husband's half. This is why the deeds must be checked first.
What If the Deceased Gave Property Away Before Death?

If a father transferred land to his daughter through a legally effective deed of gift, that land may no longer be part of his estate. The deed and retained interests must be examined.

Section 35 of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance also includes a rule called collation. Certain substantial lifetime benefits given to a child to establish them in life may need to be taken into account in calculating inheritance. Not every small gift is covered; the statute contains qualifications and exceptions.
What About Money in Bank Accounts?

Some deposits form part of the estate, but a valid nomination can change the treatment. Section 544 of the Civil Procedure Code covers nominations of specified financial assets, including qualifying bank deposits and other interests. A nomination may take effect despite a different instruction in a will.

For example, a validly nominated daughter may receive a qualifying deposit under the nomination rather than the ordinary division of the estate. Not all accounts are treated alike; the relevant account and nomination must be examined.

In particular, it is important to distinguish between an ordinary bank balance and a financial interest covered by a valid statutory nomination. The relevant account terms and documents must be reviewed.
What About Insurance and Business Assets?

Section 554A of the Civil Procedure Code excludes certain insurance money and nominated financial assets from estate property for testamentary proceedings. Company shares owned personally by the deceased may form part of the estate; assets owned by the company itself do not automatically become personal property of the shareholder. Partnership agreements and other documents may also matter.

A business partnership may require examination of the partnership agreement and the deceased's interest in it. Insurance proceeds may be paid under their own statutory and contractual arrangements.
Do Debts Affect the Estate?
Yes. Mortgages, loans and other enforceable obligations must be considered before distribution. An heir should not assume inherited property is free of security or other liabilities.
What Documents Should Be Collected?

Preserve deeds, survey plans, financial and investment records, nomination forms, insurance documents, vehicle registrations, loan agreements and any will. Avoid transferring or disposing of assets before establishing their legal position.

A property investigation or title search may be necessary where the ownership history is uncertain. Avoid assuming that possession of a deed proves exclusive ownership.
Conclusion
Identify the estate before dividing it. Joint ownership, lifetime transfers, nominations, business interests and debts can all alter what is actually available for inheritance.
legal: Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance, sections 21, 22 and 35
articles.intro: When someone dies, family members often begin discussing who should inherit the house, land or savings. But before deciding who receives what, there is an important question: what property actually belonged to the deceased? Not everything connected to a deceased person necessarily forms part of the property available for inheritance. Understanding this distinction can help prevent misunderstandings and disputes.

articles.title: Does Everyone Inherit Property Under the Same Law in Sri Lanka?
articles.seo: Different Inheritance Laws in Sri Lanka
articles.description: Understand the differences between general inheritance law, Kandyan law, Thesawalamai and Muslim law in Sri Lanka.
articles.dek: Why similar families may inherit different shares under Sri Lanka's legal systems.
sections: Why Are There Different Inheritance Laws?

Two families may each have a father who died without a will leaving a wife, children and land, yet the same inheritance formula may not apply to both. Sri Lanka's law developed through general law, customary laws and legislation. The principal systems are general law, Kandyan law, Thesawalamai and Muslim law.

These rules developed from a combination of general law, customary law and legislation. They should not be treated as interchangeable, and the relevant legal system should be identified at the beginning of the inquiry.
1. General Law of Inheritance

The Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance provides the general intestate rules. A surviving spouse ordinarily receives one-half, with children and other descendants taking priority in distributing the remainder. For example, a wife and two children ordinarily receive one-half, one-quarter and one-quarter respectively, assuming the general law governs the distributable estate.
2. Kandyan Law

Kandyan law contains distinct inheritance rules under legislation including the Kandyan Law Declaration and Amendment Ordinance and the Kandyan Succession Ordinance. It distinguishes certain categories of property, including paraveni ancestral or inherited immovable property and acquired property.

It also contains rules regarding surviving spouses' life interests and, in specific contexts, binna and diga marriages. A life interest generally permits enjoyment or use during a person's lifetime without necessarily granting full ownership. These provisions require individual application, not the automatic use of the general-law one-half spouse rule.

Residence in the Central Province alone does not establish that a deceased person was governed by Kandyan law. Its application must be legally determined.
3. Thesawalamai

The Jaffna Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance provides important rules for persons governed by Thesawalamai. The origin and category of property, including ancestral interests, may affect inheritance; in some circumstances a link to the father's or mother's side matters.

Not every Tamil person is automatically governed by Thesawalamai. Its applicability is a legal question, not a conclusion based only on ethnicity, surname or present address.

In particular, property associated with different family lines may be dealt with differently under the relevant provisions. It is necessary to examine the person's status as well as the origin and character of the property.
4. Muslim Law

The Muslim Intestate Succession Ordinance provides for the application of the Muslim law governing the sect of the deceased where its statutory conditions are satisfied. It has distinct rules concerning spouses, children, parents and other relatives. Do not apply the general-law half-share formula automatically to a Muslim estate.
What If the Deceased Left a Will?

The Wills Ordinance, as amended in 2022, recognises broad testamentary freedom, but a will's validity and legal effects must be considered under the law relevant to the particular circumstances.

Intestate succession rules should not simply be used to calculate the distribution where a legally effective will disposes of the relevant property.
What If the Deceased Lived Abroad?

International estates may involve additional rules. Under section 21 of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance, succession to immovable property situated in Sri Lanka is distinguished from movable property, for which domicile may matter. Domicile is not necessarily the same as nationality or temporary residence.
How Can the Family Identify the Applicable Law?

Consider the deceased's legally relevant status, family and marriage history, domicile, type and location of property, and any will. Do not calculate shares merely from religion, surname or present address.
Conclusion
There is no single intestate inheritance formula for every Sri Lankan family. Establish the applicable law before deciding who inherits and in what proportions.
legal: Kandyan Law Declaration and Amendment Ordinance
Jaffna Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance
articles.intro: Two Sri Lankan families may experience similar circumstances. In both families, a father dies without leaving a last will. Each father leaves a wife, children and land. But does the law necessarily divide their property in the same way? No. Sri Lanka has different legal systems governing inheritance. This is important to understand before calculating shares in a deceased person's property.

articles.title: Can Parents, Brothers, Sisters and Grandchildren Inherit Property in Sri Lanka?
articles.description: Learn when parents, siblings and grandchildren can inherit property under Sri Lanka's general intestate succession law.
articles.dek: Practical examples of inheritance rights beyond the surviving spouse and children.
sections: Who Has the First Right to Inherit?

Under general intestate succession law, children and other descendants take priority over parents, siblings and more distant relatives, subject to the surviving spouse's statutory rights. Certain exceptions and rules of representation apply.

The statutory order is important: a more distant relative cannot ordinarily inherit alongside a closer category where the law gives that category priority. The surviving spouse's entitlement must also be considered.
Can Grandchildren Inherit?

Yes. Suppose a grandmother had two children: a daughter who is alive and a son who died before her, leaving two children. The grandmother dies without a spouse or will. Under general law, the daughter ordinarily receives one-half and the two grandchildren share the deceased son's half, receiving one-quarter each.

This is called inheritance by representation. Grandchildren do not automatically take equal shares alongside their living parent.
What If Both Parents of the Deceased Are Alive?

If a married man dies with no descendants but leaves his wife and both parents, under general law his wife ordinarily receives one-half and the father and mother one-quarter each. This assumes the full estate is subject to general intestacy.
What If Only One Parent Survives?

Under section 25 of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance, one surviving parent may share with qualifying siblings of the deceased. For example, where a person dies leaving no spouse or descendants, but a mother and one full brother, the mother would ordinarily receive half and the brother the other half.

The result may change where full or half-siblings or descendants of deceased siblings are involved. Section 25 includes a qualification where no qualifying sibling is alive at the deceased's death: in that situation the surviving parent may take the whole relevant portion even if descendants of deceased siblings survive.

This is why it is important to examine exactly who was alive on the date of death and to distinguish siblings of the whole blood from certain half-siblings.
Can Brothers and Sisters Inherit?

Yes, where the statutory order permits it. Sections 26–29 distinguish full siblings from half-siblings and make particular provision for paternal and maternal relationships. Equal division among everyone called a sibling may therefore be wrong.
What About Uncles, Aunts and More Distant Relatives?

More distant relatives may inherit when closer statutory classes have failed. Section 31 deals with remoter ascendants and collateral relatives; further provisions address cases where no qualifying heirs remain. Exact relationships must be established.

Where no qualifying relatives remain, the law also makes provision for the ultimate destination of the property. A person's closeness in everyday family life does not alone determine succession rights.
Can an Adopted Child Inherit?

A valid adoption can give important inheritance rights. Section 6 of the Adoption of Children Ordinance generally treats an adopted child as a child born in lawful wedlock of the adopter, subject to statutory qualifications. Particular inheritance issues involving the adopter's wider family, older instruments or special laws require separate consideration.
What About Children Born Outside Marriage?

Section 33 of the Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance uses historical statutory terminology and contains particular rules affecting maternal and paternal intestate succession. Legal parentage, other legislation and the applicable legal system must be examined. It would be misleading to assume all cases produce identical rights without a legal assessment.
What If the Family Disagrees?

Gather birth, marriage, adoption and death records, establish all relevant relationships and apply the correct law before asserting shares or transferring property.

Uncertain parentage, missing documents and disputes about a deceased sibling's descendants may require closer investigation. It is safer to establish the family tree and legal entitlement before making property transfers.
Conclusion
Parents, siblings, grandchildren and more distant relatives can inherit in appropriate cases, but closeness of relationship alone does not settle entitlement. The statutory order matters.
legal: Matrimonial Rights and Inheritance Ordinance, sections 23–36
articles.intro: When someone dies without a last will, the surviving husband, wife and children are usually the first family members considered. But what if the deceased had no children? Can their parents inherit? Do brothers and sisters have rights? What happens when a child died before their parent, leaving grandchildren? Sri Lanka's general inheritance law provides rules for these situations.

articles.title: How to Make a Legally Valid Last Will in Sri Lanka
articles.seo: How to Make a Valid Will in Sri Lanka
articles.description: Understand how to make a legally valid last will in Sri Lanka, including witnessing, notarial requirements and executors.
articles.dek: The legal formalities, documents and choices that matter when making a will.
sections: Who Can Make a Last Will?

Under the Wills Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 29 of 2022, a person who has reached 18 years of age may make a will within the scope of the legislation. The testator must also have the necessary mental capacity and act voluntarily. A will may be challenged if the person lacked capacity or was subject to legally impermissible pressure.

In particular, a person's capacity must exist when the will is executed. Being at least 18 years old is not the only legal requirement.
What Property Can Be Included?

A will can deal with land, houses, bank balances, investments, vehicles and other legally disposable interests. A person cannot ordinarily give away another person's property. If a husband and wife each own half a house, a will by the husband cannot ordinarily dispose of the wife's half.
Can a Parent Leave Everything to One Child?

The Wills Ordinance, as amended in 2022, recognises broad freedom to choose beneficiaries, including excluding a particular relative without assigning reasons. But testamentary freedom does not remove requirements concerning validity, capacity, ownership and proper execution.
How Should a Last Will Be Signed?

The Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, as amended by Act No. 30 of 2022, prescribes requirements for an ordinary will, including a written document, signature, the prescribed thumb impression or statutory alternative, and execution before a notary public and two witnesses present at the same time. Notarial rules must also be observed.

Older guidance suggesting a will can simply be executed before five witnesses without a notary is not a reliable statement of the amended law. Professional assistance is advisable.
What Should the Will Contain?

• Clear identification of the testator and beneficiaries.
  • Accurate property descriptions.
  • The intended gifts or shares.
  • A suitable executor.
  • Contingencies if a beneficiary dies first.
  • A provision for the remaining estate.

A residuary clause deals with property left after specific gifts and liabilities. Without an effective clause, some assets may pass under intestacy.

For example, a testator may leave a specific house to a daughter and direct how the balance of the estate should be divided. The will should also deal with what happens if a beneficiary dies before the testator.
Who Should Be the Executor?
Choose a reliable person capable of obtaining probate, protecting assets, dealing with debts and distributing the estate. The executor is not automatically the owner of the property.
Can a Beneficiary Sign as a Witness?

Section 11 of the Prevention of Frauds Ordinance contains rules affecting gifts made to an attesting witness or that witness's spouse. This can affect a benefit intended under the will. Suitable independent witnesses can help avoid this problem.
Can a Will Be Changed?

A person may wish to change a will after marriage, having children or acquiring property. A new properly executed will, a codicil or another recognised method may be needed. Informal crossing-out or handwritten changes to an executed will may not work. Marriage may also affect an existing will.

Major changes in family circumstances, including marriage, divorce or the birth of children, are sensible occasions to review existing testamentary arrangements.
Where Should the Will Be Kept?

Keep the original securely and ensure the executor or a trusted person knows where it can be located. Missing originals can make probate more difficult.

Where the original cannot be found after death, proving the deceased's wishes can involve additional evidentiary and court difficulties.
Conclusion
A valid will requires much more than written wishes. Proper drafting, execution and safekeeping help families understand and implement the testator's intentions.
legal: Wills Ordinance, section 2, as amended by Act No. 29 of 2022
Prevention of Frauds Ordinance, sections 4, 6, 7 and 11, as amended
articles.intro: Many people believe that making a last will is something to think about only when they become elderly. Others assume that writing down their wishes, signing the paper and keeping it safely at home is enough. However, a last will must meet specific legal requirements to be valid. A properly prepared will can help someone decide how their property should be distributed after death and reduce uncertainty for their family.

articles.title: Can a Last Will Be Challenged in Court in Sri Lanka?
articles.seo: Challenging a Last Will in Sri Lanka
articles.description: Learn when a last will can be challenged in Sri Lanka, including forgery, undue influence, capacity and court procedures.
articles.dek: Unfairness alone is not enough. Understand the grounds and evidence that matter.
sections: Is an Unequal Inheritance a Reason to Challenge a Will?

A father dies leaving most of his property to one child. Others think this is unfair. Under the Wills (Amendment) Act, No. 29 of 2022, a person has broad freedom to decide who inherits, including excluding relatives. An unequal gift is not automatically unlawful. The real question is whether the will was legally valid.
What If the Person Lacked Mental Capacity?

A testator must have the required testamentary capacity when making the will. Serious illness or cognitive impairment can raise questions, but old age or physical illness alone does not establish incapacity. Medical evidence and testimony concerning the person's understanding at the time may matter.

The central question is the testator's actual understanding when the document was made. Witnesses, medical evidence and the surrounding circumstances may be relevant.
What If Someone Pressured the Deceased?

A will may be disputed if it resulted from legally impermissible threats or pressure. Ordinary affection, closeness or persuasion does not necessarily amount to undue influence. Evidence about what happened is essential.
What If the Signature Was Forged?
Fraud and forgery can undermine a will. Relevant evidence may include the original document, genuine signatures, notarial records and the testimony of attesting witnesses. An allegation is not proof.
What If the Will Was Not Properly Signed?
Mandatory signature, impression, notarial and witnessing requirements must be observed. The requirements in force at the time the will was executed must be identified.
What If Circumstances Look Suspicious?

If a major beneficiary organised the will, kept it secret or was unusually involved in execution, the circumstances may deserve scrutiny. Such involvement does not automatically prove invalidity; the evidence must be examined to establish genuine testamentary intentions.

For example, unusual secrecy or substantial involvement by a beneficiary may call for closer examination, but neither fact automatically proves a will invalid.
Who Can Challenge a Will?

A person ordinarily needs a sufficient legal interest in the estate, such as an heir whose rights would be affected or someone claiming under another will. Unrelated persons cannot generally object merely from disagreement.
What Evidence May Be Important?

• The original will and earlier or later wills.
  • Notarial and witness evidence.
  • Relevant medical records.
  • Documents proving title.
  • Evidence of alleged pressure, fraud or forgery.
  • Relevant communications and surrounding circumstances.
When Should Objections Be Raised?

The Civil Procedure Code provides notice and objection procedures during probate. Section 536 provides for caveats in appropriate cases. A caveat is a formal procedural step by someone seeking to oppose a grant. Interested persons should act promptly.

Anyone with a genuine basis to contest the application should preserve documents and seek timely legal assistance instead of relying on informal accusations.
Can Probate Be Challenged After It Has Been Granted?

In specified circumstances, sections 537 and 538 allow applications to recall or revoke a grant. A completed probate cannot simply be reopened because a relative changes their mind; legal grounds and the prescribed procedure are required.
Can Mediation Help?

Family members may be able to negotiate practical issues such as occupation or sale of inherited property. Mediation cannot replace a court determination that a disputed will is valid or dispense with statutory steps. Any agreement must respect the rights of affected persons.

Possible practical arrangements may concern occupation of the family home, sale of jointly inherited land or distribution of sentimental belongings. A mediator cannot by agreement prove a forged instrument genuine or replace statutory probate procedure.
Conclusion
A will may be challenged for recognised reasons such as fraud, forgery, lack of capacity, undue influence or improper execution—not merely because the distribution seems unfair.

articles.intro: A father dies leaving most of his property to one child. The other children believe the arrangement is unfair. One claims the father was seriously ill when the will was signed. Another suspects the beneficiary pressured him. Can the children challenge the will? Yes, but a will cannot be set aside merely because someone is unhappy with their inheritance. There must be a legally recognised reason.

articles.title: How to Obtain Probate in Sri Lanka: A Step-by-Step Guide
articles.seo: How to Obtain Probate in Sri Lanka
articles.description: A practical guide to obtaining probate in Sri Lanka, including the application, notice procedure, court order and executor's duties.
articles.dek: What an executor should know about proving a will in the District Court.
sections: Step 1: Find the Original Last Will

After a mother dies leaving a will, the family should locate the original document. It may be held by a notary, lawyer, relative or another custodian. Section 516 of the Civil Procedure Code requires a person holding or finding it after death to produce it to the proper District Court as soon as reasonably possible, with the required information.

The accompanying affidavit and information about the death and estate should be prepared as required. A family member holding the will should not simply leave it in a drawer indefinitely.
Step 2: Identify the Executor
The will normally names an executor to administer the estate. If that person cannot or will not act, an eligible person may seek letters of administration with the will annexed.
Step 3: Find the Correct District Court

Under the Code, jurisdiction may relate to where the deceased lived at death, where the executor lives or where land belonging to the estate is situated. The correct court must be identified before filing.
Step 4: Prepare the Application

Section 524 requires a petition and affidavit giving relevant details of the will, estate property, heirs and the applicant's entitlement, with evidence of proper execution. The section specifies a period of three months from the date the will is found for the application. If there has been delay, obtain legal advice on its implications.

A petition is a formal request to court; an affidavit is a sworn written statement. The application should identify the estate and relevant heirs to the applicant's knowledge.
Step 5: Publish the Required Notice

Section 529 requires a prescribed newspaper notice in Sinhala, Tamil and English on two separate occasions in consecutive months. Interested persons can object. The objection date is set within the statutory period of 60–67 days from the first publication. Probate therefore cannot ordinarily be completed immediately after the petition is filed.
Step 6: What If Nobody Objects?

If no objections are made, the court considers the evidence. Where it is satisfied, it may declare the will proved and direct the grant of probate under section 531. The legal requirements must still be met even in an unopposed application.
Step 7: What If Someone Objects?
Objections may concern alleged forgery, lack of capacity, improper execution or the applicant's entitlement. The court may hold an inquiry. An objection alone does not prove the will invalid.
Step 8: Take the Oath and File the Inventory

Following the relevant order, section 539 requires the executor's prescribed oath within fifteen days and an inventory and valuation within one month after the oath. The grant issues in accordance with the statutory procedure.

The inventory and valuation record the property subject to administration. They are not mere formalities; the executor must account for their handling of the estate as required by law.
Step 9: Administer the Estate

The executor must protect and collect assets, address valid debts, distribute according to the will and maintain records. Section 551 also contains accounting requirements. Probate is authority to administer, not personal ownership.

The executor may also need to complete land-registration or other asset-transfer documents after addressing valid liabilities. The grant is not necessarily the end of the process.
What If the Original Will Is Missing?

Section 540 provides for limited grants in certain exceptional circumstances, including particular lost-will situations. A photocopy should not automatically be treated as sufficient evidence without examining the law and facts.
What If the Executor Lives Overseas?
The Code contains provisions under which a duly constituted attorney or other eligible person may act in particular circumstances. The power of attorney and court requirements must be examined.
How Long Does Probate Take?

There is no single timeframe. Publication, evidence, objections and court scheduling affect the process. A contested will may take substantially longer than a properly documented and unopposed application.
Conclusion
Probate requires production of the will, a court application, prescribed notices, an order, and compliance with oath and inventory requirements. Preparation helps avoid preventable delays.
articles.intro: A mother dies leaving a last will. In it, she names an executor and states how her house, land and other property should be distributed. The family now wants to know what happens next. In Sri Lanka, the executor may need to obtain probate through the appropriate District Court. Probate is the formal grant through which the will is proved and the executor's authority is recognised.

articles.title: How to Obtain Letters of Administration in Sri Lanka: A Step-by-Step Guide
articles.seo: Letters of Administration in Sri Lanka
articles.description: Learn how to obtain letters of administration in Sri Lanka, identify legal heirs and follow the District Court procedure.
articles.dek: A practical court-procedure guide for families dealing with an estate without a will.
sections: What Are Letters of Administration?

A father dies without a will, leaving a house, vehicle and bank account. His family may need letters of administration: a court grant authorising an administrator to deal with the estate. The administrator gathers assets, deals with debts and distributes the remainder according to law. The grant does not mean that the administrator inherits everything.

The administrator is a representative of the estate, not the person entitled to take every asset. They must deal with the property and liabilities in accordance with the court grant and law.
Step 1: Identify the Legal Heirs

Find out whether the surviving spouse, children, parents or other relatives are entitled to inherit. Determine whether general law or a special system such as Kandyan law, Thesawalamai or Muslim law governs. Collect relevant birth, marriage, death and adoption records.
Step 2: Identify Property and Debts

Prepare accurate details of land, buildings, bank balances, vehicles, investments and other assets, together with mortgages, loans and creditors. This information is needed for the application and administration.
Step 3: Determine Who Should Apply

Section 526 of the Civil Procedure Code permits an interested person to seek letters of administration. In competing claims, section 523 gives preference to the surviving widow or widower, although the court may depart from it for good cause. A widow appointed administrator does not thereby extinguish her children's inheritance rights.

For example, a widow may obtain administration even though her three adult children also have inheritance rights. These are separate legal questions.
Step 4: Check the Estate's Value

Section 525 contains a reporting duty where a person dies in Sri Lanka without a will leaving property in Sri Lanka valued at Rs. 4 million or more, subject to the section's conditions. The surviving spouse or next of kin must report the death within one month. Section 527 also addresses administration of such estates.

Do not assume that a smaller estate never needs a court document or that its land may be transferred without considering succession rules.
Step 5: Prepare the Court Application

Section 528 provides for a petition and affidavit setting out the death, absence of a will, heirs, estate property, liabilities, creditors, applicant's entitlement and agreed shares where relevant. The section specifies three months from the date of death for making the application. Seek advice if that period has passed.

Where shares are agreed and relevant, the application should include those details. Failure to disclose relevant heirs or creditors may give rise to procedural difficulties.
Step 6: Notify Other Interested Persons

The relevant next of kin must be identified. Written consents may be obtained, and the prescribed procedure for notifying non-consenting respondents must be followed. Concealing another legal heir can create serious complications.
Step 7: Publish the Notice

Section 529 requires publication on two separate occasions in consecutive months and provides an opportunity for objections. If unopposed and the evidence is sufficient, the court may make an appropriate order under section 531. Disputes may require an inquiry.
Step 8: Obtain the Grant

Under section 539, after the order the administrator takes the prescribed oath within fifteen days and files an inventory and valuation within one month after that oath. Letters are issued under the statutory procedure.
Step 9: Administer and Distribute

The administrator protects property, addresses valid liabilities and distributes the balance to entitled heirs while observing accounting duties. The estate is not the administrator's personal property.
Can the Family Obtain Certificates of Heirship Instead?

Sections 526 and 531 permit eligible heirs to seek certificates identifying heirs and their agreed shares in appropriate intestate cases. However, the court may determine that active administration and letters are necessary instead.

These certificates may help heirs prove their entitlement to particular inherited interests. But where active administration is required, certificates alone may not be sufficient.
What If There Are Debts or Disputes?

Valid creditors must be considered before distribution. Insolvent estates may involve separate statutory provisions. Heirs may object through the prescribed process; lawful negotiation may resolve practical differences but cannot replace required court or land-transfer formalities.

The Civil Procedure Code has provisions for administration of insolvent testamentary estates. Agreements among heirs cannot remove valid creditor rights or compulsory transfer requirements.
Can Heirs Sell the Property?

Section 545 restricts certain estate-property transfers within a specified five-year period. The date of death, estate value, existence of a will, form of grant and nature of the transaction can matter. Have the title and required documents examined before sale.
Conclusion

Letters of administration provide a lawful means of dealing with an intestate estate. Identifying heirs and assets, filing properly, notifying interested persons and following the court process helps protect everyone concerned.
legal: Civil Procedure Code, sections 523, 525–545, and provisions concerning insolvent testamentary estates
articles.intro: A father dies without leaving a last will. He owned a house, a vehicle and some money in a bank account. His wife and children know that they may be entitled to inherit his property, but they are uncertain how to deal with the estate legally. In such circumstances, the family may need letters of administration issued by the appropriate District Court.
